Event description: The Battle for Hill 3234 was fought by Soviet Troops in Afghanistan to secure an important strategic road. 39 Soviets faced 250 well-armed Mujahideen rebels over the course of two days, suffering heavy casualties but ultimately prevailing.

The Livgarde (Royal Guard) represents one of Europe’s oldest extant military formations. Their existence dates back to the origins of modern Sweden itself. In the present day, they are now modernised and mechanised, but at the core, they haven’t changed.

In exile, King Karl XII and his Swedes had been guests of the Ottoman Sultan Ahmed III for nearly three and a half years. They had outstayed their welcome and the skirmish at Bender commenced. It was all deemed a misunderstanding that led to the fight and the tragic loss of men.

Event: Final Carolean death march survivors return home
Event description: After Carolus Rex was killed, Carolean soldiers were ordered to retreat home to Sweden. An ill-fated decision to march 6,000 defeated troops across Norway’s Tydal mountains resulted in almost two thirds of the men freezing to death on their journey.

At the legendary Battle of Thermopylae in Ancient Greece, King Leonidas and a small number of soldiers – including 300 of his warriors from the state of Sparta – died making an heroic last stand against an invading force of around 100,000 Persians.

John McCrae was a military doctor and a Major of the 1st Brigade of Canadian Field Artillery. His famous poem, 'In Flanders Fields' immortalised the dying in Flanders and the Great War. He wrote this poem after witnessing the death of a dear friend. The poppy flowers he wrote of became the universal symbol of remembrance.

The Satsuma Rebellion was the last revolt of the samurai against the imperial government of emperor Meiji. Ending with the famous Battle of Shiroyama, the uprising marks the final chapter of Japan’s most famous warriors.

Major Yevdokia Bershanskaya was commander of the 588th Night Bomber Regiment of the Soviet Air Force – the all-female regiment known as the Night Witches, who carried out stealthy anti-German bombing activity from 1942 until the end of WWII.

Event: Stalin orders deployment of Night Witches
Event description: Women were originally barred from combat in the Soviet Union, until Josef Stalin ordered the deployment of three female flying regiments, one of which was the 588th Night Bomber Regiment, nicknamed the "Night Witches" for their stealthy attacks.
The Battle of the Somme was one of the Great War’s bloodiest battles. It took place from July 1 and November 18, 1916, between the armies of the British and the French against the German Empire.

Event: First call for British volunteer soldiers
Event description: When the First World War broke out, thousands of volunteers flocked to army recruitment offices of their respective armies to do their bit for their countries and be part of what they thought would be a short, grand adventure. A sizable portion of these volunteers were young teenagers and underage boys aged 13-16, who would sadly never return home.

On December 24, 1945, Ian Fraser Kilmister, known as the legendary Lemmy, was born in England. He was the founder, lead singer, bassist and main songwriter of Motörhead, one of the most influential bands in music history. Lemmy died on December 28, 2015, at the age of 70.

In 1906, the HMS Dreadnought was officially launched at sea. This mighty battleship was armed with greater speed, greater range and larger guns than any other vessel. In battle, it would remain untouched, staying out of range of the lighter guns of its foes.

The Great War began in July 1914 and concluded in November 1918. It was the very first global conflict that spanned multiple continents and oceans from Europe, Africa and Asia to the Indian Ocean, and North and South Atlantic Oceans. Territory was lost, and gained, empires crumbled and millions sacrificed their lives to fight.

Scotland was embroiled in a war with England for its independence when the Scots besieged Stirling Castle. The mighty English force that was sent to end the siege was humiliated at Bannockburn by a much smaller Scottish army, led by Robert the Bruce.

In 1918, the Harlem Hellfighters were assigned to fight in WW1 alongside the French army. This regiment was mainly made up of African American soldiers, and they were not allowed to fight alongside the ordinary American soldiers.

Fraustadt was one of Sweden’s greatest victories in the Great Northern War, when the Swedes – outnumbered by more than 2:1 – used a perfectly-devised pincer movement tactic to entrap their opponents and capture or kill three quarters of their force.

The Battle of Passchendaele was one of WWI's major campaigns on the western front. Raging from July 31 to November 10, 1917, the fights between Allied forces and the Germans in Flanders accounted for over half a million deaths.

The Battle of Verdun lasted over 300 days. It was the longest battle of the First World War, and for many of the war’s soldiers, it was the epitome of brutal, mechanised modern war. For a few kilometres of land, hundreds of thousands of men lost their lives.

The Battle of the Yser, which took place during WWI, began on October 16, 1914. The Entente and the Belgians successfully crushed the Germans’ hopes of continuing the Schlieffen Plan. Each attempt was foiled by entrenched machine guns and artillery, as well as by the deliberate flooding of the Yser Canal, which affected the German trenches.

Event: The Battle of Belleau Wood begins
Event description: During the Battle of Belleau Wood, US Marines had taken the fight to the enemy and were ready to accept heavy casualties to achieve victory against the Germans. The ferocity of the attack earned them the name 'Devil Dogs'.

Event: Charles XII buried at Riddarholmen Church
Event description: Nearly three months after his death at the Siege of Fredriksten, King Charles XII (Carolus Rex) was buried at Riddarholmen Church, the historic resting place of Swedish monarchs. Having never married or fathered children, he was succeeded by his sister.

France’s Albert Severin Roche became known as “The First Soldier” of France for his heroism and bravery. Despite his small stature and his peers’ scepticism, by the end of WW1 Albert had more than proved himself, having captured over 1,180 prisoners while fighting for the French Army.
Gustavus Adolphus was perhaps Sweden’s greatest king: a pioneer of modern warfare and statesmanship who laid the foundations for the Swedish Empire and many elements of the modern Swedish state.

Francis Pegahmagabow concluded WWI as one of only 37 Canadian soldiers to receive two bars on their Military Medals and was the most highly decorated aboriginal soldier in Canadian history. He was credited with 378 sniper kills and he captured over 300 prisoners.

Operation Gunnerside was one of the most successful sabotage missions in history. By blowing up a production facility at Norway’s Vermork Hydroelectric Plant, the saboteurs thwarted Hitler’s efforts to produce the materials needed for an atomic bomb.

A celebrated Serbian war hero, Milunka Savić is one of the world's most decorated female combatants who fought in both Balkan Wars and WWI. She is known for cutting off her hair and changing her appearance to look like a man in order to take her brother’s place in the army.

Led by King Gustav II Adolf, the Swedish army took on the Catholic League and the Habsburg Imperial Army on September 17, 1631, in an open field near the village of Breitenfeld. After seven hours of battle, the Swedish-Saxon army was victorious.

Following the complete failure of the Austro-Hungarian invasion of Serbia in 1914 during World War I, it was time for the Imperial army to try again the following year. On October 9, 1915, the fall of Belgrade was declared.

Event: First Stormtrooper unit authorised on the Western Front
Event description: The Stormtroopers were specialist soldiers of the German Army who used precise infiltration tactics to target their enemies during WWI. During their assaults they would apply a deadly mix of shock, surprise and ultra violence.

Event: Sir Adrian Carton de Wiart dies
Event description: A man with war in his blood, Sir Adrian Carton De Wiart was of Belgian heritage but fought for the British Empire during WW1. Throughout his stints at war, he was injured multiple times, and despite the severity of his wounds, survived. He became known as the ‘man who could not be killed’.

The people of Bohemia disliked their childless king’s choice of heir and elected their own prince. When the appointed heir sent representatives to Prague Castle, rebels threw them from a window, starting Europe’s bloodiest pre-20th Century war.

Thomas Edward Lawrence, known as the legendary Lawrence of Arabia, was deemed by the British public as a modern-day Robin Hood. His tale was a tale of courageous fighting, of distant journeys and exotic oriental adventure. He was assigned to the British officer corps in Egypt and was renowned for his role in the Arab Revolt and the Sinai and Palestine Campaign against the Ottoman Empire.

Alvin York led the 82nd Infantry Division against the German defensive machine gun nests on Hill 223 in 1918 and captured a large group of German Soldiers. York became one of the biggest American heroes. He scooped countless medals, including the Congressional Medal of Honor. He died on September 2, 1964, of a cerebral haemorrhage at the age of 76.

The last major clash of the Thirty Years’ War happened in the same place as the first: Prague. With final peace negotiations underway, Sweden took the opportunity for a last assault on Bohemia to loot Prague Castle and seize its prized art collection.

Fritz Haber’s inventions truly benefited the world. He helped billions of people, yet his inventions also caused terrible, agonising deaths and lifelong suffering for hundreds of thousands during World War I. He is responsible for the advent of chemical warfare.

Event: ‘The Red Baron’ Manfred von Richthofen dies
Event description: A great symbol of World War I, Manfred Albrecht Freiherr von Richthofen, known as The Red Baron, was a killer in the skies. On April 21, 1918, his red triplane came to a stop and he was killed by a single bullet through the heart.

The Belgian Armed Forces unit, whose motto is “Resist and Bite”, is known for its fierce resistance against Germany’s invasion of Belgium in WWII. Panzer division commander Erwin Rommel said of their bravery: “They are not men; they are green wolves”.

Event: Charles XII of Sweden is crowned
Event description: Charles XII of Sweden, or Carolus Rex, ascended to the throne at age 15. He was a strong believer in the divine right of kings and spent his whole life at war to expand or protect the Swedish Empire.

In the early morning of August 6, the German gas batteries opened up and a dark green smog crept over the Russian lines at Osowiec Fortress. Despite the deadly effects of the poison gas, the Russians, like dead men returning to life, counterattacked the German infantry.

The Wehrmacht was the united armed force of Germany, comprising the Heer (army), Kriegsmarine (navy) and Luftwaffe (air force). It was established by Hitler in direct disregard of the restrictions on German rearmament that were imposed after WWI.

The Battle of Flers-Courcelette on September 15, 1916, saw the very first tank take on the battlefield. The first tank on tank battle took place on April 24, 1918, during The Second Battle of Villers-Bretonneux. This deadly vehicle was the future of mechanised warfare.

This battle is widely thought to have begun the downfall of the Swedish Empire, when Peter the Great and his Russian army routed the Caroleans on a battlefield in modern day Ukraine. Carolus Rex, wounded, spent five years in exile after the defeat.

In the summer of 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand planned a visit to Sarajevo to present himself to the Bosnian people. On June 28, 1914, he and his wife, Sophie Chotek von Chotkowa, were assassinated. It was an event that would change the world forever, leading to the downfall of four mighty empires.

Event: Col di Lana summit taken by the Italians
Event description: At 23:30 on April 17, 1916, the Italians, who were up against the Austro-Hungarian Empire, detonated 5,000kg of Nitro-Gelatine. Around 200 Austrian soldiers were killed in the explosion and the following assault, and the Italians secured the Col di Lana summit.

Event: The second Battle of Doiran begins
Event description: During the Battles of Doiran (in 1916, 1917 and 1918), the Bulgarians tenaciously defended their well prepared positions against British troops. Three times the attackers went up against the lines and three times they were beaten back.

The Sack of Rome occurred when disaffected Holy Roman Empire troops attacked the city in search of spoils. The outnumbered Swiss Guard, protectors of the Vatican, stood against the invading horde, giving their lives so the Pope could make his escape.

An act of trust during World War I, on December 24, 1914, an unofficial Christmas Truce was enforced on the Western Front. British and German soldiers united, mingled and even played games together - a rare but magical moment of peace.

Three Brazilian soldiers were attacked by German troops while on patrol in Montese, Italy. Refusing to surrender, they fought until their ammunition ran out. The Germans, impressed by the heroes (Helden), buried the men with a cross by their graves.

The Treaty of Versailles was one of five treaties signed by the Central Powers that ended the First World War. It was considered the most important and was formalised on June 28, 1919, in the Palace of Versailles. The Treaty comprised the 'War Guilt clause', which required Germany to cede territory, pay reparations and disarm.

Vienna was a key goal for the Ottoman Empire, which was at war with Europe for centuries. After besieging the city for two months, the Ottomans were driven away when a relief force, including the famed Winged Hussars of Poland, arrived to save Vienna.

Event: The Black day of the German Army
Event description: Known as “the black day of the German army”, 530 British tanks broke into the German lines in Amiens, France, achieving major breakthroughs for the first time in years, heralding the beginning of the end of World War I.

Manowar's first album, 'Battle Hymns', was released in 1982. The band took the world by storm and for over 40 years they have celebrated the essence of True Heavy Metal. Manowar still holds the record for being the loudest band in history.

Operation Typhoon kicks off on October 2, 1941. Despite the brutal weather conditions, the German offensive continues its ruthless advance on Moscow. Half a million Muscovites are forced to prepare for battle to defend their city against the enemy.

For two days, 150 British and colonial soldiers defended Rorke’s Drift mission station in South Africa from up to 4,000 Zulu warriors. Leader John Chard and 10 of his men were awarded the Victoria Cross medal – the most ever given for a single action by one regiment.

German general of the 12th Army, Walther Wenck, realised the end of the war was approaching. Instead of attempting to defeat the invading Soviet forces during the Battle of Berlin, which he was ordered to do, he used his army to create an escape corridor out of Berlin. He was responsible for up to 250,000 people escaping to safety.

Event: First trenches dug on the Western Front
Event description: The First World War kicked off on July 28, 1914, and ended on November 11, 1918. This war marked the start of trench warfare. Due to the heavy artillery and machine guns used on the Western Front, armies were forced to dig trenches to protect themselves.

The First World War ended on November 11, 1918. It is estimated that 9,722,000 soldiers had been killed, while 21 million others had survived the war but were left scarred or maimed for life. It is also estimated that 6-13 million civilians perished in the conflict.

An American Army captain, a Waffen SS officer and a German Army Major made a plan to rescue and defend French hostages from loyal Nazis at Castle Itter in Austria. All of the hostages survived the battle, thanks to one of the least likely alliances of World War II.

Disregarding a treaty formed in WWI, Hitler sends Bismarck, Germany's mightiest battleship, on a secret mission to the Atlantic. Following a merciless battle with the British navy, it sinks on May 27, 1941. Out of more than 2,000, only 115 of its crew survive.

On Armistice Day in 1920, an unknown British soldier was symbolically buried to commemorate those who lost their lives during World War I. These soldiers were never identified or laid to rest. Each year, the site attracts thousands of pilgrims and tourists.

In October 1918 during the Meuse-Argonne Offensive, 554 all-American soldiers, who were part of the 77th Division, were completely surrounded by the German army. Known as ‘The Lost Battalion’, the soldiers were also subjected to friendly fire. Only 194 of them made it out alive.

This extraordinary Polish soldier bravely entered Auschwitz to gather intelligence, becoming Inmate 4859. He escaped two years later and went on to fight in the Warsaw Uprising, but was later executed for spying by Poland’s new communist government.

After lying about his age to enlist, Audie Murphy became one of the most decorated US soldiers of WWII. He went on to act in Hollywood, but died in a plane crash aged just 45. His grave at Arlington Cemetery is the most visited after John F Kennedy’s.
Rob Halford is the vocalist of the legendary heavy metal band, Judas Priest. The band has left an unforgettable stamp on the history of Heavy Metal and continues touring and rocking to this day.

Event: The Charlie Brown and Franz Stigler incident
Event description: Following the bombing of the city of Bremen, Germany, Charlie Brown's B-17 bomber, ‘Ye Old Pub’, has suffered heavy damage. As he and his men scramble to get back to England, German fighter ace Franz Stigler begins his attack but shows them mercy.

Six months after the attack on Pearl Harbor, the US Navy delivered a decisive defeat to Japan in a four-day battle near Midway Atol in the Pacific. The battle severely weakened Japan’s navy and is considered a turning point in WWII in the Pacific.

Leslie “Bull” Allen was an Australian soldier who was awarded the US Silver Star for single-handedly rescuing 12 injured Americans at the battle of Mount Tambu in 1943, carrying each man out of the line of fire on his shoulders before returning for the next.

Lauri Törni served for three armies during his remarkable military career: first for his birth country of Finland, then he joined the Nazi SS to fight against the Soviets, and finally, he emigrated to the USA to fight for the American Army. He died in a helicopter crash in Vietnam.

Karel Janoušek was an heroic Czech airman who played a key role in the Battle of Britain, only to be imprisoned in his own country after the war. Our song Far From the Fame commemorates Janoušek and the sacrifices he made.

The Battle of Britain was the first major campaign fought entirely by air forces, in which the Royal Air Force defended the island against the Luftwaffe. Despite the name, almost one in five fighter pilots who flew for Britain were from overseas.

The Warsaw Uprising was a major insurrection by the Polish Resistance, taking place from August 1st to October 2nd 1944. Trying to liberate the city from its German oppressors, the Uprising symbolises the bravery of the Polish people.

Event: The liberation of Paris military battle
Event description: In mid-August 1944, the Allied offensive in France had broken through the German lines in Normandy. Local resistance groups emerged from the underground, supporting the Allies with important intelligence and harassing the retreating German soldiers.

The Greco-Italian war took place from October 28, 1940, until April 23, 1941. Prior to it kicking off, the Greeks were given an ultimatum – to permit Italy’s occupation of certain strategic points or face war. They chose to stand their ground and fight heroically.

The Greco-Italian war took place from October 28, 1940, until April 23, 1941. Prior to it kicking off, the Greeks were given an ultimatum – to permit Italy’s occupation of certain strategic points or face war. They chose to stand their ground and fight heroically.

Event: End of the Siege of Bastogne
Event description: Men from the US 101st Airborne Division (the Screaming Eagles) were sent to defend Bastogne from approaching Nazi troops. With the town surrounded and cut off from supplies, they fought for seven days in bitter cold before reinforcements arrived.

Event: Kristallnacht – The Night of Broken Glass
Event description: Kristallnacht, also known as the ‘Night of Broken Glass’, was a pogrom against Jewish communities in Germany. 1,000 synagogues and prayer rooms were vandalised or set on fire, while 7,500 shops were destroyed and looted. Jewish neighbourhoods were attacked and 90 Jews were killed.

Simo Häyhä was arguably the most prolific sniper of all time, earning the nickname “White Death” following up to 505 kills in the Finnish Winter War. Although seriously wounded just before the war ended, he went on to become a hunter and lived to the age of 96.

Event: Erwin Rommel assumes command of 7th Panzer Division
Event description: The 7th Panzer Division of the German Army earned its nickname “Ghost Division” for its skilful surprise attacks during the WWII invasion of Belgium and France. Erwin “Desert Fox” Rommel was one of its most successful and famous commanders.

The ancient Yinqeshan Han tombs were accidentally discovered by Chinese construction workers. They contained a treasure trove of well-preserved 2,000-year-old bamboo writing tablets – including chapters from Sun Tzu’s 'The Art of War'. The Art of War consists of 13 chapters, each of which highlights a different aspect of warfare.

In the early days of the Nazi invasion of Poland – the event that started WWII – a few hundred brave Poles mounted a three-day defence against more than 40,000 Germans, a battle that has drawn comparisons to the famous last stand of the Spartans.

The Soviet Partisan movement sprang up after Germany’s invasion of the USSR. Up to 6,000 resistance groups carried out activity ranging from guerrilla attacks to delivering anti-Nazi propaganda. A unified HQ for the movement was launched in 1942.

The Gallipoli campaign was a long and controversial attempt to reach and occupy Constantinople (Istanbul) during WWI. The doomed campaign cost 44,000 allied troops their lives, more than a quarter of whom were from Australia and New Zealand.

Event: Start of the Finnish Winter War
Event description: This conflict saw a tiny but adaptable Finnish Army hold off a mighty Soviet force for several weeks before efforts were redoubled and they were overrun. The resulting peace treaty would see Finland forced to cede large amounts of land to their invaders.
In 1943 during World War II, one of the largest tank battles in history resulted in the Soviet Union gaining the advantage on the Eastern Front, which it would hold until the end of the war.

On July 24, 1943, Operation Gomorrah began. On the evening of July 27, a fleet of 730 British bombers appeared over the city unleashing over 2,300 tons of bombs on Hamburg. Major fires broke out all over the city causing a lethal storm of fire. Dresden was the next target in 1945.

Event: Official opening of restored Gokstad mound
Event description: The discovery of the Gokstad burial mound in Norway granted a glimpse into the world of Vikings. Following its excavation in 1880, a ship buried 1,000 years earlier was found, and next to a large pile of shields, swords and jewellery lay a man who was the embodiment of a Viking. In July 1929, an official opening ceremony was held which was attended by King Haakon VII and thousands of spectators.

The Battle of Berlin was the last major offensive of World War II in Europe and saw the Soviet Army capture the German capital. Hitler and several senior Nazis would commit suicide before the battle was over, and Germany’s surrender would follow.

Event: Harry Truman sworn in as US President
Event description: Just hours after Harry Truman was sworn in as the US President, he was led to a meeting and informed of the real purpose of the secret Manhattan Project. Using electromagnetic separation, the nation's top scientists had uncovered a way to create weapons of mass destruction.

There was no glorious ending for the man responsible for the bloodiest war in human history. With the German capital Berlin crippled by a massive Soviet attack and on the verge of falling, Hitler retired to his study and shot himself.

On September 11, 2001, a group of Arab Jihadists led by Osama bin Laden hijacked four commercial airliners and crashed them into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. The act of terrorism resulted in the death of 2,996 people.

The Srebrenica Massacre began on July 11, 1995, and concluded on July 22, 1995. Over 8,000 Bosniak Muslim males between the ages of 12 and 77 were captured and brutally executed. It was considered the bloodiest massacre and crime against humanity Europe had seen since the end of WW2.

The 1982 Falklands War was a two month conflict between Argentina and the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic. The UK retained control of the islands, but both countries continue to claim sovereignty over them to this day.

United Nations Day is a global day of celebration, marking the day representatives from 50 countries met to sign the charter that established the UN. Sabaton’s song A Light in the Black is about peacekeeping – just one part of the UN’s international work.

The birth date for Heavy Metal might as well be February 13, 1970, when Black Sabbath dropped their groundbreaking debut album, which took the blues-heavy Rock n Roll sound of the late 60s and put a harder, gloomier and occult spin on things.

The famous landings on the beaches of Normandy started Operation Overlord, the Allied invasion of German-occupied France. Winning this crucial battle gave the Allies a foothold from which to start pushing back the Nazis and turning the tide of WWII.

Operation Overlord, the Allied invasion of Nazi-occupied France, began with the D-Day beach landings. After a slow start the Allies pushed the Germans back until Paris was liberated and the Germans retreated across the River Seine.

The Gulf War began on August 2, 1990 and concluded on February 28, 1991 after 1,000 hours of war in the air and 100 hours of fighting on the ground. 35 nations, led by the USA, had defeated Iraq, which was armed with one of the largest armies on the planet.

Merchant ship convoy ON 92, en route to America from Britain, was detected by Wolfpack Hecht, a group of Nazi U-boats (submarines) patrolling the north Atlantic. Seven ships were sunk before the Wolfpack lost contact with them on May 13.

Already fragile peace in the Middle East was broken when Egypt closed a major shipping canal to Israeli vessels. Israel declared war, launching pre-emptive airstrikes. Jordan and Syria intervened, but all three nations were defeated, losing 20,000 troops.

The largest battle in war history was an attempt by the Axis powers of WWII to capture the city of Stalingrad. The invaders were repelled by Soviet forces, but not before the city was destroyed and up to 2 million people killed, wounded or captured.

Officially a war between North and South Vietnam, countries around the world became involved, most notably the USA. Nearly 60,000 US troops died, and some tactics used in the war – such as chemical defoliation – remain controversial to this day.

The Purple Heart is a medal given to US Armed Forces members who have been wounded or killed by enemy action. The first Purple Heart was awarded to Army Chief of Staff General Douglas MacArthur, who spearheaded the design and launch of the medal.

Event: Judas Priest releases debut album “Rocka Rolla”
Event description: On September 6, 1974, Judas Priest unleashed their debut album 'Rocka Rolla'. They proudly embodied the old working-class flair of their hometowns and defined the sound of Heavy Metal with the fast-paced power of double guitars.

In August 1914, Europe marched to war. The sound of heavy boots moving in unison could be heard, while proud banners flew above the soldiers. A short war was anticipated but a short war was not what they got.

The Battle of Monte Cassino began on January 17 and concluded on May 18, 1944. It entailed four Allied assaults against the Winter Line (a series of German and Italian military fortifications) in Italy during WWII. The battle resulted in 55,000 Allied deaths and 20,000 killed and wounded Germans.

For two days, 150 British and colonial soldiers defended Rorke’s Drift mission station in South Africa from up to 4,000 Zulu warriors. Eleven defenders were awarded the Victoria Cross medal – the most ever given for a single action by one regiment.

Event: Charles XI of Sweden was born
Event description: King Charles XI of Sweden reigned until his death in 1697. He was fundamental to the development of the Caroleans, who were considered the elite warriors of Europe in their day. They won great battles with their innovative and superior tactics.
